audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the Wright 1906 sec. 12 deciding quotation (p. 7) and the Braune 1891 secs. 9/55/75 corroborating quotations are verbatim in the held archive.org scanned files at the stated places. (2) Deciding source: a 1906 pedagogical primer backed by the 1891 edition of the standard reference grammar (Braune). For a dead corpus language there is no instrumental literature; the best current description is Braune/Heidermanns 17th ed. 2023 (not yet obtained, paywalled; verified via CrossRef). Glottolog lists only Wright as a grammar. publisher pages (De Gruyter, DNB) were bot-blocked. (3) downloaded the open-access Fulk 2018 comparative grammar; its sec. 2.2 confirms the classification exactly: fixed initial (root) stress, verbal prefixes unstressed

sources.citation: Wright, J. (1906). An Old High German Primer. Oxford: Oxford University Press. 170 pp.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Stress (Accent). 12. In all uncompounded words the chief stress falls upon the stem-syllable and always remains there even when suffixes and inflexional endings follow it. This syllable is always the first of the word. In compound words the chief stress falls upon the stem-syllable of the first component part if the second part is a noun or an adjective; and on the stem-syllable of the second part if this is a verb or derived from a verb.
sources.locator: Grammar ch; I sec. 12 'Stress (Accent)', printed p. 7
sources.note: Sec. 12 is the whole statement: fixed chief stress on the stem-syllable, which in uncompounded words is always the first syllable; the only exception given is compounds whose second member is a verb or deverbal (stress on the second member's stem, i.e. verbal prefixes unstressed). No secondary stress stated, no weight condition, no tone. Related: sec. 10 (printed p. 7, p. 23) says the sonantal vowel bears the stress and all OHG diphthongs ei, ie (ea, ia), io (eo), iu, ou (au), uo (ua) were falling, stress on the first element; sec. 72 note (printed p. 31, p. 47): in primitive Germanic

sources.citation: Fulk, R. D. 2018. A Comparative Grammar of the Early Germanic Languages (Studies in Germanic Linguistics 3). Amsterdam: John Benjamins. Open access, DOI 10.1075/sigl.3.
sources.quote: 'When the accent shifted in Proto-Germanic, in most lexical categories it came to rest on the initial syllable of the word ... The prefix *ga-/*gi- is never stressed, but other prefixes on nouns and adjectives were usually stressed ... The chief exception to the rule of initial stress is that verb roots receive primary stress, leaving prefixes unstressed or with a lesser degree of stress. The chief evidence for root-stress in verbs is of two kinds: alliterative patterns in verse and vowel reductions in prefixes.' n. 5: 'variation in the spelling of the OHG equivalent (fur-, for-, fir-, fer-) c
sources.locator: Ch. 2 'Prosodic Features and the Syllable', sec. 2.2 'Lexical accent in Proto-Germanic', pp. 36-37 ( lines 2248-2333, incl. n. 5 on OHG prefixes)
sources.note: Modern open-access comparative grammar covering OHG; sec. 2.2 (pp. 36-37) restates initial stress with unstressed verbal prefixes and stressed nominal prefixes, citing OHG prefix-vowel variation -- a 2018 corroboration to add beside Wright 1906/Braune 1891.

sources.citation: Sievers, Eduard. 1920. Steigton und Fallton im Althochdeutschen mit besonderer Beruecksichtigung von Otfrids Evangelienbuch. In: Aufsaetze zur Sprach- und Literaturgeschichte. Wilhelm Braune zum 20. Februar 1920 dargebracht von Freunden und Schuelern, 148-198. Dortmund: Ruhfus.
sources.note: Schallanalyse study: rising vs falling syllable pitch in OHG texts is sentence-melodic/declamatory and said to govern doublet spellings; accent marks read as melodic. No lexical tone claimed.

tone.quote: Von dem, was wir Satzmelodie nennen, kommt für unsere Spezialzwecke insbesondere dreierlei in Betracht, was wir unter die Schlagworte Tonrichtung, Tonbindung und Tonlage bringen können. In ersterer Beziehung, also hinsichtlich der Tonrichtung, sind Steigton und Fallton zu unterscheiden. ... so bezeichne ich im folgenden den Steigton durch Akut, den Fallton durch Gravis (also hábe mit in sich steigendem, hàbe mit in sich fallendem a: natürlich ohne alle Rücksicht auf dynamische Verhältnisse). ... Der Gegensatz zwischen Steig- und Fallton ist ja großenteils deklamatorischer Natur: man muß also auch Otfrids Verse richtig deklamieren lernen, um zu glaubhaften Resultaten zu gelangen.
tone.locator: pp. 150-151 and p. 161, untitled introduction before section I. Zur Behandlung der Geminaten
tone.translation: Of what we call sentence melody, three things in particular matter for our special purposes, which we can bring under the headings tone direction, tone binding and tone level (pitch register). As to the first, tone direction, rising tone and falling tone are to be distinguished. ... so in what follows I mark the rising tone with an acute, the falling tone with a grave (thus hábe with internally rising, hàbe with internally falling a: of course without any regard to dynamic relations). ... The contrast between rising and falling tone is, after all, largely declamatory in nature: one must therefore learn to declaim Otfrid's verses correctly in order to reach credible results.
tone.summary: Schallanalyse study: rising vs falling syllable pitch in OHG texts is sentence-melodic/declamatory and said to govern doublet spellings; accent marks read as melodic. No lexical tone claimed.

sources.citation: Armitage, Lionel. 1911. An Introduction to the Study of Old High German. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
sources.note: Historical grammar: pitch (musical) accent attributed to Indo-European; Germanic accent fixed and primarily stress. Nothing on pitch in OHG itself; Notker's ^ and ` mark long/short accented vowels.

tone.quote: Doubtless in the main the variation of sound is due to variation of stress accent, for in the IG. and the early Gmc. period this accent was free ... while in duration it was either acute (δέα) or slurred (δεᾶς). ... But not all variations can be accounted for in this way ; there are others which are probably due to IG. having had, beside the stress accent, also a pitch or musical accent, which seems to have predominated towards the close of the period, though in Gmc. the accentuation became again primarily one of stress. Thus a distinction has to be made between grade of stress (quantitative grade) and grade of pitch (qualitative grade).

sources.citation: Sievers, Paul. 1909. Die Accente in althochdeutschen und altsächsischen Handschriften (Palaestra 57). Berlin: Mayer & Müller.
sources.note: A complete survey of acute/circumflex accent marks in OHG and OS manuscripts (four usage types, Notker's system as the consistent one). Conclusion p. 123: the accents are 'Tonzeichen' = marks of word accent (Betonung, i.e. stress, on the stem syllable, as in Latin grammatical practice), only secondarily quantity marks (Type I: circumflex on long, acute on short stressed vowels). 'Ton/Hochton' here is the philological term for stress; no pitch/tonal contrast is posited. Results section then lists what the accents attest for OHG Quantitaet (pp. 123-128) and Betonung (pp. 128-132: secondary stre…

tone.quote: Die Frage nach der Bedeutung der Accente im Althochdeutschen und Altsächsischen wird am richtigsten beantwortet werden: sie sind Tonzeichen (wie im Lateinischen), meist auf Stammsilben gesetzt, erst sekundär sind sie auch Zeichen der Quantität, die in ihren Funktionen manchmal noch zu trennen (Typus I: Circumflex auf Länge, Acut auf Kürze), meist aber nicht mehr reinlich zu scheiden sind (Typus II. III. IV). ... [p. 122] wenn der Circumflex im Deutschen, abweichend vom Lateinischen, auch auf die antepaenultima und noch weiter nach vorn gerückt werden konnte, also der Tonsilbe zustrebte, die in der Regel die Stammsilbe war.
tone.locator: p. 123 (and p. 122), 'Ergebnisse' following the survey of accent material; Betonung results pp. 128-132
tone.translation: The question of the meaning of the accents in Old High German and Old Saxon is best answered thus: they are accent marks [signs of the (stress) accent] (as in Latin), mostly placed on stem syllables; only secondarily are they also signs of quantity, functions that can sometimes still be separated (Type I: circumflex on a long, acute on a short vowel) but mostly can no longer be cleanly distinguished (Types II, III, IV). ... since the circumflex in German, unlike Latin, could be moved onto the antepenult and further forward, i.e. it gravitated to the accented syllable, which as a rule was the stem syllable.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Accent marks = stress (stem/initial syllable) + vowel quantity; no tonal contrast described.

S.: Buchdruckerei des Waisenhauses, 28 pp. (partial print; the full study appeared in Zeitschrift fuer deutsche Philologie 14 (1882): 129-172, 285-300 -- journal pages from a search-result citation, not seen on the volume itself).
sources.note: Reads Notker's acute/circumflex as marks of vowel quantity plus word stress (Hauptton on first/root syllable, Nebenton by rhythm); 'ton' = accent, pitch never discussed. At least 20 accented forms.

tone.quote: Wie wir schon oben erwähnten, wird in den ältesten ahd. denkmälern nur der circumflex, aber nicht consequent, angewendet zur bezeichnung einer grammatikalischen länge. Er ist daher ursprünglich kein accentus, sondern ein auf die quantität sich beziehendes grammatikalisches zeichen. Aber zu dieser bestimmung hat er sehr bald noch eine zweite übernommen, die bezeichnung eines hervorgehobenen tones ... Wir werden also zwei funktionen der accente zu unterscheiden haben: die bezeichnung der quantität der silben und die bezeichnung der hervorhebung einer silbe im ton.
tone.locator: p. 4, sec. 1 'Die accente und die ahd. betonung'
tone.translation: As we mentioned above, in the oldest OHG monuments only the circumflex is used, though not consistently, to mark a grammatical length. It is therefore originally not an accentus but a grammatical sign referring to quantity. But to this function it very soon added a second one, the marking of a prominent tone [accent] ... We shall thus have to distinguish two functions of the accents: the marking of the quantity of syllables and the marking of the prominence of a syllable in tone [accent].

tone.quote: 2. Aber woher der Anfangsakzent? (Vgl. Scherer S. 80 ff.) Der grammatische Wechsel setzt die Verschiebung der idg. Tenues, also zugleich exspiratorischen und idg.-freien Akzent voraus. Das ergibt eine Übergangs-Periode, in der der idg. durch den sekundären exspiratorischen Anfangsakzent erdrückt, eine vorwiegend musikalische von einer vorwiegend exspiratorischen Betonung abgelöst wird, wie das z. B. am Italischen, Keltischen und später am Griechischen zu beobachten ist ... [§ 55] so ist es der exspiratorische Charakter des Akzents, der hier wirksam ist, d. h. auch die hochdeutsche Tenuisverschiebung ist noch eine Folge der germanischen Festlegung des Anfangsakzentes
tone.locator: sec. 153 'Schluß', p. 253; sec. 55 'Die Tenuisverschiebung', p. 92-93; sec. 6 'Akzent', p. 17
tone.translation: 2. But where does the initial accent come from? (Cf. Scherer p. 80 ff.) Verner alternation presupposes the shift of the IE tenues, hence an accent that was already expiratory and still IE-free. This yields a transitional period in which -- the IE accent being crushed by the secondary expiratory initial accent -- a predominantly musical accentuation is replaced by a predominantly expiratory one, as can be observed e.g. in Italic, Celtic and later in Greek ... [sec. 55] it is the expiratory character of the accent that is at work here, i.e. the High German tenues shift too is still a consequence of the Germanic fixing of the initial accent.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Expiratory (dynamic) word-initial stress accent; IE musical accent replaced; no tone.
